question: Q03
answer: Three notes together: note-gaussian-noise-least-squares shows that maximizing the likelihood under i.i.d. Gaussian noise is exactly minimizing the sum of squared residuals; note-map-estimation-priors shows MAP = log-likelihood + log-prior, and that an isotropic Gaussian prior θ ~ N(0, τ²I) contributes −‖θ‖²/(2τ²), so with the Gaussian-noise likelihood MAP becomes 'squared error plus a constant times ‖θ‖²' (constant σ²/τ²); note-ridge-regression-penalty is exactly that objective, ‖y − Xw‖² + λ‖w‖². Link in one paragraph: least squares is the negative log-likelihood of a Gaussian-noise model; adding a zero-mean Gaussian prior on the weights adds its negative log-density, which is a squared-norm penalty; so the ridge objective is the negative log-posterior and its minimizer is the MAP estimate, with λ = σ²/τ² — a narrow prior (small τ) is a large λ, a flat prior (τ → ∞) gives back plain least squares. This also answers the open question in your ridge note ('Where does λ come from … does it mean something?'): it is the noise-to-prior variance ratio. (The Laplace prior in the MAP note gives the lasso's Σ|θ_j| instead.)

evidence.quote: argmax_w log L(w) = argmin_w Σ_i (y_i − wᵀx_i)²
the whole thing is squared error plus a constant times ‖θ‖², with the constant being σ²/τ² after rescaling
L(w) = ‖y − Xw‖² + λ‖w‖²
Where does λ come from — is it just a knob you tune by cross-validation, or does it mean something?

question: Q16
answer: In note-svm-kernel-trick, a kernel is a function k(x_i, x_j) = φ(x_i)ᵀφ(x_j) that replaces the inner products x_iᵀx_j in the SVM dual, giving a linear separator in φ's feature space without ever computing φ (e.g. RBF k(x,x') = exp(−γ‖x − x'‖²), an infinite-dimensional φ); a function is a valid kernel iff every kernel matrix it produces is positive semi-definite (Mercer). Not the OS kernel or a CNN convolution kernel — your Garden seed kernel-is-an-overloaded-word lists those other meanings. Kernel methods beyond the definition are deferred as out of exam scope.
